parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones to ask about joining a community choir.
script: Hello, Riverside Community Choir, Helen speaking.
Hi. I saw your advert, and I'm interested in joining the choir.
Wonderful. We're always looking for new members. Can I take your name?
Arjun Mehta. M, E, H, T, A.
Thank you. Do you know what type of voice you have?
I think I'm a tenor. That's what my music teacher said, anyway.
Great, we need more tenors. Have you sung in a choir before?
Only at school, but that was a long time ago.
That's fine. We don't hold auditions. We rehearse every Tuesday evening, from seven thirty until nine thirty.
In St Mark's church hall, on Hill Street. There's plenty of parking.
Yes, it's forty pounds per term. That covers the hall and the pianist.
Do I need to buy any music?
We lend all the music, but we ask everyone to buy a black folder, so we all look the same at concerts.
In December, just before Christmas. So if you start now, you'll have plenty of time to learn the pieces.
Who should I speak to on my first evening?
Our musical director, Simon Grey. That's G, R, E, Y. He'll show you where to sit.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide introduces visitors to a botanic garden.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Westbridge Botanic Garden. My name's Ian, and I'm one of the volunteer guides.
The garden was founded in 1680, not as a public park, but as a place for doctors and students to grow plants used in medicine. It only opened to the public in the nineteenth century.
Today, our most visited attraction is the Palm House, the large Victorian glasshouse you can see behind me.
Unfortunately, we won't be able to cross to the island today, because the bridge is being repaired.
At the end of your visit, you might like to stop at the shop, where you can buy seeds collected from plants here in the garden. We don't sell live plants, I'm afraid.
Let me tell you about some areas you shouldn't miss. The Desert House contains cactuses and other plants from very dry regions of the world.
The Physic Garden is where it all started. It contains plants that have been used in medicine for centuries, with labels explaining their uses.
The Sensory Garden is designed for people to touch and smell the plants. It's especially popular with children and visitors with visual impairments.
In the Water Garden, the main attraction is the pond with giant water lilies, whose leaves can be over two metres wide.
The Woodland Walk is home to the garden's tallest tree, a giant redwood planted in 1860.
And finally, the Butterfly House, which opened only this year. It's already very popular, so you may have to wait a few minutes to get in.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two psychology students, Elena and Theo, discuss their experiment on music and memory.
script: Elena, let's go over our experiment on music and memory before we write it up.
OK. Our hypothesis was that background music with lyrics would reduce people's ability to remember information.
Right, because the words in the song compete with the words being learned. We tested thirty volunteers from the university sports club.
Yes. Each person had to remember a list of twenty words, in three conditions.
One problem I noticed was that some participants already knew the pop song we used. A few of them even started singing along, which might have affected the results.
True. We should mention that as a limitation. And I think our next step should be to repeat the experiment with a larger group, maybe a hundred people.
Agreed. Let's check the results. In silence, the average number of words recalled was fourteen.
With classical music, it was thirteen, so almost no difference.
But with the pop song with lyrics, it dropped to nine.
Interesting, though, that seventy percent of participants said they prefer studying with music.
Which suggests people don't realise how it affects them. For the next stage, I'd like to try nature sounds, like rain.
Good idea. Rain sounds are very popular with students.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of vaccination.
script: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at the history of vaccination, one of the most important developments in the history of medicine.

Our story begins with smallpox, a disease that killed around three hundred million people in the twentieth century alone. Long before vaccines, people noticed that those who survived smallpox never caught it again.

This led to a practice called variolation. Material from the sores of a person with a mild case was inserted into a small cut in the skin of a healthy person, who usually developed a mild form of the disease and became immune. It was practised for centuries in China, India and Africa, and in the eighteenth century it was brought to Britain from Turkey by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu.

Variolation was risky, though. Some people died. In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner tested an observation made by country people: milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, did not catch smallpox. Jenner showed that infecting someone with cowpox protected them. The word vaccine comes from the Latin word vacca, meaning cow.
In the nineteenth century, Louis Pasteur extended the idea, developing a vaccine for rabies in 1885.

The greatest success came in 1980, when the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated, the first human disease to be completely eliminated. Polio may be next: cases have fallen by more than ninety-nine percent since 1988.

Recent technology has changed how vaccines are made. During the COVID-19 pandemic, mRNA vaccines, which give cells instructions to make a harmless protein from the virus, were developed in less than a year.
The challenge today is often not science but trust. Vaccine hesitancy, where people delay or refuse vaccination, has led to outbreaks of diseases such as measles in several countries.

passages.title: The Story of Coffee
paragraphs: According to a popular legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia by a goat herder named Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became unusually energetic after eating the red berries of a certain bush. It is a charming story, but it was first written down in 1671, many centuries after coffee drinking began, and historians treat it with caution.

The earliest reliable evidence of coffee drinking comes from Yemen, across the Red Sea from Ethiopia, in the fifteenth century. There, members of Sufi religious communities drank coffee to help them stay awake during night-time prayers. Yemen soon became the centre of the coffee trade, and much of the world's supply passed through its port of Mocha, a name still used for coffee today.

By the sixteenth century, coffee houses had spread to cities such as Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul. They became important places for conversation, music, games and the exchange of news, and were sometimes called 'schools of the wise'. Not everyone approved. At various times, religious and political authorities tried to close coffee houses, fearing that they encouraged criticism of those in power.

Coffee reached Europe in the seventeenth century, arriving first in Venice, where the first coffee house opened in the 1640s. England's first coffee house opened in Oxford in 1652, and within a few decades London had hundreds. Like their Middle Eastern predecessors, they were centres of business and debate. One, owned by Edward Lloyd, became a meeting place for ship owners and merchants, and eventually developed into the insurance market Lloyd's of London.

For a long time, Yemen tried to keep control of coffee production, but plants were eventually taken elsewhere. In the late seventeenth century, the Dutch smuggled plants out and began growing coffee on the island of Java, in present-day Indonesia. In 1714, the Dutch gave a coffee plant to the French king, and descendants of that plant were later taken to French colonies in the Caribbean. From there, coffee spread to Central and South America. Since the 1840s, Brazil has been the world's largest producer.

Today, coffee is grown in more than seventy countries, and the livelihoods of millions of small farmers depend on it. However, climate change poses a serious threat. Arabica coffee, which accounts for most of the world's production, grows best within a narrow range of temperatures, and some studies suggest that the area suitable for growing it could fall by around half by 2050.

passages.title: Why We Laugh
paragraphs: Laughter is older than language. Chimpanzees, gorillas and other apes make a breathy, panting sound when they play and tickle each other, which researchers regard as the ancestor of human laughter. Even rats produce high-pitched calls when tickled. This suggests that laughter evolved long before humans, as a signal that behaviour is playful rather than threatening.

Surprisingly, most human laughter has little to do with jokes. The psychologist Robert Provine spent many hours recording when people laughed in everyday situations. He found that the great majority of laughter followed ordinary remarks, such as 'I'll see you later' or 'Look, it's Andre', rather than anything particularly funny. He also found that people are around thirty times more likely to laugh when they are with others than when they are alone.

These findings suggest that laughter is above all a social signal. Laughing together helps people to bond and shows that they share an understanding. The psychologist Robin Dunbar has argued that laughter triggers the release of endorphins, chemicals in the brain that produce feelings of pleasure and wellbeing. In one study, people who had watched a comedy video together could tolerate more pain afterwards than those who had watched a documentary, which Dunbar interpreted as a sign of endorphin release.

Laughter is also highly contagious. Hearing someone else laugh makes us more likely to laugh ourselves, which is why television comedies have long used laugh tracks. The neuroscientist Sophie Scott found that the sound of laughter activates areas of the brain that prepare the face to move, as if the brain is getting ready to join in.

Laughter is often said to be good for health, and some people now practise 'laughter yoga', which was developed in Mumbai in 1995 and involves laughing deliberately in groups without jokes. Some studies have found that laughter can reduce stress and temporarily improve mood, but evidence for longer-term health benefits is limited, and many claims are exaggerated.

Although what people find funny varies greatly between cultures, the sound of laughter itself appears to be understood everywhere. In a 2010 study, researchers played recordings of emotional sounds to members of the Himba, a group in Namibia with little contact with Western culture. The Himba easily recognised laughter produced by British people as an expression of amusement, suggesting that it is a universal human signal.

passages.title: Do Zoos Still Have a Place?
paragraphs: For most of history, collections of wild animals were symbols of power. Ancient rulers in Egypt, China and Rome kept menageries of exotic creatures to display their wealth and influence, and the animals' welfare was of little concern. Modern zoos present themselves very differently. Most now claim three main purposes: conservation, education and research.

Their conservation record includes some genuine successes. The Arabian oryx, a desert antelope, was extinct in the wild by 1972, but animals bred in zoos were successfully reintroduced to Oman ten years later, and the species now survives in the wild again. The California condor had fallen to just 22 birds by 1987, when all of them were taken into captivity for breeding. Today the population numbers more than 500, many of them flying free. Without zoos, I believe neither species would exist today.

However, not all animals cope well with captivity. Species that naturally travel long distances, such as elephants and polar bears, often show signs of stress in zoos, including stereotypic behaviour: repetitive actions such as pacing, swaying or swimming in circles. A major study of elephants found that those in European zoos had considerably shorter lives than elephants in protected areas in the wild. No matter how well designed, an enclosure cannot replace a range of hundreds of kilometres.

Claims about education are also open to question. Zoos argue that seeing real animals inspires visitors to care about wildlife, but studies of visitor behaviour suggest that most people spend less than a minute at each enclosure and rarely read the information provided. Whether a brief look at a tired tiger changes anyone's attitude to conservation is far from clear.

It is also worth noting that only a minority of animals in zoos belong to threatened species. Many popular zoo animals, such as meerkats and many types of monkey, are not endangered at all, and are kept mainly because visitors enjoy seeing them.

In my view, zoos can still be justified, but only if they change. They should stop keeping species that cannot thrive in captivity, such as elephants and polar bears, and focus on animals for which captive breeding can make a real difference. Above all, they should spend a far greater share of their income on protecting animals in the wild. A zoo that contributes to saving species in their natural habitats deserves our support; one that simply displays animals for entertainment does not.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the population, in millions, of three cities between 1950 and 2050, with projections from 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph shows the population of Northport, Riverton and Eastvale from 1950 to 2025, together with projections up to 2050.

Overall, all three cities grew during the period shown, but at very different rates. Riverton experienced by far the most rapid growth and is expected to become the largest city, whereas Northport's population is projected to fall slightly after 2025.

In 1950, Northport was the largest city, with 6 million inhabitants, twice as many as Eastvale, while Riverton had only 1 million. Northport grew steadily to 11 million by 2000 and 12 million in 2025, but it is expected to decline to 11 million by 2050.

Riverton, by contrast, expanded dramatically, overtaking Eastvale by 1975 and almost matching Northport in 2000, at 10 million. It had become the largest of the three by 2025, with 18 million people, and is projected to reach 26 million by 2050. Eastvale grew more gradually, from 3 million to 8 million in 2025, and is expected to reach 10 million by the end of the period.

task2.text: Some people believe that children should start learning a foreign language at primary school rather than secondary school. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages? Write at least 250 words.
model: In many countries, children traditionally began learning a foreign language at secondary school, at around the age of eleven or twelve. Increasingly, however, schools are introducing languages much earlier. In my opinion, the advantages of starting at primary school clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

The strongest argument for an early start is that young children are often better at acquiring the sounds of a new language. Children who begin early are more likely to develop natural pronunciation, and they are usually less afraid of making mistakes than teenagers, who can be self-conscious about speaking in front of their classmates. Starting early also means that learners have more years of study in total, which is important for reaching a high level. In addition, learning another language at a young age can increase children's awareness of other cultures and help them see their own language more clearly.

There are, however, some potential drawbacks. Primary school timetables are already full, and time spent on a foreign language may reduce time for basic literacy and mathematics. A further problem is the shortage of qualified teachers: if primary teachers have weak language skills themselves, children may learn incorrect pronunciation and grammar. Finally, the benefits of an early start may be lost if secondary schools fail to build on what children have already learned.

These difficulties are real, but they can be solved through good planning. Governments can invest in training primary teachers, keep lessons short and playful, and make sure that primary and secondary programmes are connected.
In conclusion, although introducing languages early requires resources and careful planning, I believe the benefits for pronunciation, confidence and long-term achievement make it worthwhile.

speaking.cue:
Describe a place you would like to visit in the future.
You should say:
- where it is
- how you know about it
- what you would do there
and explain why you would like to visit it.
speaking.cueModel: A place I'd really love to visit is Iceland. I first became interested in it a few years ago when I watched a documentary about the northern lights, and since then I've seen so many photos of its landscapes that it's become a kind of dream destination for me. What attracts me is that it seems so different from Bangladesh. Instead of flat green fields and crowded cities, Iceland has volcanoes, glaciers, black sand beaches and huge waterfalls, and the whole country has a population smaller than one district of Dhaka. If I went, I'd want to hire a car and drive around the ring road that goes around the whole island, stopping to hike and take photos. I'd definitely want to walk on a glacier with a guide, and I'd love to swim in one of the natural hot springs. And of course, I'd try to see the northern lights, which means going in winter, when it's dark for most of the day. The main reason I'd like to go, I think, is that it would be a complete change from everything I know. I love trying new things, and standing on a glacier or next to a volcano would be an experience I'd remember for the rest of my life.
